Darkened
DAR-kend
v. (past part.)
From dark, Saxon deorc. Webster 1828: made dark; deprived of light; obscured; rendered dim or gloomy. Scripture uses it of the sun at judgment, of the failing eye in old age, and above all of the understanding of men who suppressed what they knew of God.

Biblical Definition

Darkened in the New Testament is chiefly a description of the fallen mind, and Paul uses it twice with clinical precision. Romans traces the sequence: Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened (Romans 1:21). The order is critical. The darkening is not the starting point but the result — they knew, they refused to glorify, they refused thanks, and then the heart was darkened. Suppression of known truth issues in incapacity to see it. Ephesians states the same condition as the settled state of the unregenerate: Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart (Ephesians 4:18), and again the ignorance is traced back to a blindness of heart rather than a want of evidence. The word also belongs to the last day, when the created lights fail at the coming of the Son of man: Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven (Matthew 24:29).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DARKENED as made dark; deprived of light; obscured; rendered dim, gloomy, or less clear; and figuratively, rendered ignorant, blind, or unintelligible.

expand to see more

DARKENED, pp. — Made dark; deprived of light; obscured; made dim or gloomy.

Rendered less clear or intelligible; obscured in meaning; as, counsel darkened by words without knowledge.

Rendered blind or ignorant; deprived of spiritual or intellectual light.

Sullied; made less white or bright; clouded, as a countenance or a reputation.

From Saxon deorc, dark — the root also of darkness, darkling, and darksome.

Key Scripture

Romans 1:21 — "Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened."

Ephesians 4:18 — "Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:"

Matthew 24:29 — "Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken:"

Isaiah 59:3 — "For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, your tongue hath muttered perverseness."

Modern Corruption

Romans 1:21 says the darkening of the mind followed the refusal to glorify and give thanks, which contradicts the standing assumption that unbelief is fundamentally an intellectual problem awaiting better arguments.

expand to see more

Paul’s account is moral before it is intellectual, and the sequence cannot be rearranged. Men knew God; they did not glorify Him as God; they were not thankful; their reasonings became vain; the heart was darkened; professing themselves wise they became fools. Ingratitude appears in the chain before idolatry, which is worth sitting with. This is the ground of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity as it touches the mind: the noetic effects of sin mean that the unbeliever is not a neutral inquirer weighing evidence but a man suppressing what he already has. It also tells the church what apologetics can and cannot do. Arguments are worth making and Paul made them at Athens, but no argument regenerates; God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Ephesians 4:18 forecloses the other common view, that people are lost merely for want of information. Paul says the ignorance is in them and that it proceeds from the blindness of their heart — the organ named is not the intellect but the affections and the will. This does not make evangelism pointless; it makes it dependent. The same apostle who wrote these verses spent his life preaching, because faith comes by hearing and God is pleased to give sight through the foolishness of preaching. Matthew 24:29 sets the whole matter against its final horizon: the day comes when the created lights are darkened and no argument is needed, because the Son of man will be seen.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek skotizo (G4654), to darken, to obscure; skotos (G4655), darkness; skotoo (G4656), to be darkened; Hebrew chashak (H2821), to be dark, to grow dim.

expand to see more

Greek skotizo (G4654) — to darken; their foolish heart was darkened (Romans 1:21) and the sun be darkened (Matthew 24:29).

Greek skotoo (G4656) — to be darkened, to be blinded; having the understanding darkened (Ephesians 4:18).

Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness; the realm from which the saints are called into marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9).

Hebrew chashak (H2821) — to be or grow dark; those that look out of the windows be darkened (Ecclesiastes 12:3).

Greek porosis (G4457) — hardness, callousness; the blindness of their heart in Ephesians 4:18 is literally a callus.

Usage

"Their foolish heart was darkened (Romans 1:21) — the darkening follows the refusal to glorify and give thanks."

"Having the understanding darkened… because of the blindness of their heart (Ephesians 4:18) — the organ named is the heart."

"The sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light (Matthew 24:29) — the created lights failing at His coming."
